clinicalPearls: Causes a myeloneuropathy that closely mimics vitamin B12 subacute combined degeneration
Haematological features include anaemia and neutropenia, sometimes with ring sideroblasts mimicking myelodysplasia
Common causes are prior upper gastrointestinal surgery, malabsorption and, importantly, excess zinc intake
Zinc excess (from supplements or denture creams) induces intestinal metallothionein that blocks copper absorption
A sensory ataxia with dorsal column signs and spastic gait is typical
Copper repletion and removing the cause (for example stopping excess zinc) halt progression
reference.pathophysiology: Copper is a cofactor for enzymes essential to haematopoiesis and to the integrity of the nervous system. Deficiency, from malabsorption, prior gastric or bariatric surgery, or zinc-induced blockade of copper absorption, impairs these enzymes, producing a myeloneuropathy affecting the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts and a marrow disturbance causing anaemia and neutropenia. Excess zinc upregulates enterocyte metallothionein, which binds copper and prevents its absorption, a frequently overlooked mechanism. The neurological picture closely resembles vitamin B12 deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of sensory ataxic myelopathy
additionalInvestigations: Serum zinc (to detect zinc excess as the cause)
Full blood count and, where relevant, bone marrow examination
Vitamin B12 to exclude the main mimic
History of gastrointestinal surgery, supplements and denture-cream use
reference.prognosis: Haematological abnormalities usually recover well with copper repletion, but neurological deficits may only stabilise rather than fully reverse if treatment is delayed.
pitfalls: Overlooking zinc excess as the cause
Misdiagnosing the marrow appearance as myelodysplastic syndrome
Attributing the myeloneuropathy solely to vitamin B12 deficiency
Not checking copper in unexplained myelopathy after gastric surgery
management: Repletion with copper supplementation, orally where tolerated or intravenously in malabsorption or severe deficiency, to halt progression
Remove the precipitating cause, in particular stopping excess zinc from supplements or denture-fixative creams
Address underlying malabsorption and optimise nutrition after upper gastrointestinal or bariatric surgery, including adequate copper in enteral or parenteral feeds
Monitor treatment response with serial serum copper, caeruloplasmin and full blood count
Exclude and treat coexisting vitamin B12 deficiency, the principal clinical mimic
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy for residual sensory ataxia and gait disturbance
Refer to haematology and neurology, recognising that haematological features usually recover while neurological deficits may only stabilise if treatment is delayed
